# Best overall: BLUETTI AC200L

<row align=start gap={3}>
  <AsyncImage query="BLUETTI AC200L portable power station front view" aspectRatio="3:4" maxWidth="124px"/>
  <box flex="1" gap={1}>
    <badge color="success">Best for RVs under $900</badge>
    **<Entity value="BLUETTI AC200L" category="product" disambig="2048Wh portable LiFePO4 power station"/>**
    <title size="2xl" color="success" tabularNums={true}>$854.05</title>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">With AFF5OFF discount; $899 regular price</text>
    - 2,048 Wh LiFePO4 battery
    - 2,400 W AC output
    - Built-in TT-30 RV outlet
    - 1,200 W maximum solar input
    - 62.4 lb
  </box>
</row>

**Why I'd choose it:** The built-in TT-30 outlet is the deciding advantage for RV use. You can plug your RV's 30-amp shore-power cord directly into the station instead of relying on adapters or a separate connection solution.

According to page 2, the AC200L was in stock on BLUETTI's US website on October 31, 2026, despite being late in its product lifecycle. 

[Buy BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l)

## How the alternatives compare

Based on your supplied pages:

| Model | Capacity | AC output | RV TT-30 | Price |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| **BLUETTI AC200L** | 2,048 Wh | 2,400 W | Yes | **$854.05** |
| Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 | 2,048 Wh class | — | Yes | $899.99 |
| Renogy PowerStation 2000 | 2,048 Wh | 2,400 W | Yes | $849 |
| BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 | 2,074 Wh | 2,600 W | No | $899 |
| Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 | 2,042 Wh | 2,200 W | Not established | $899 at Jackery |

Sources: [Dealectric RV comparison](https://dealectric.com/best-2kwh-power-station-for-rv), [BuyerSheet 2kWh comparison](https://buyersheet.com/power-stations/best/2kwh/), [Jackery review](https://www.gearranking.com/power-stations/jackery-explorer-2000-v2/).

## When I'd choose something else

<row align=start gap={3}>
  <AsyncImage query="Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 portable power station" aspectRatio="1:1" maxWidth="104px"/>
  <box flex="1" gap={1}>
    **<Entity value="Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2" category="product" disambig="Portable power station"/>**

    Choose this if portability matters most. Dealectric identifies it as the lightest of the three TT-30-equipped options, at 41.7 lb. Price: $899.99.
  </box>
</row>
<divider color="subtle"/>
<row align=start gap={3}>
  <AsyncImage query="BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 portable power station" aspectRatio="1:1" maxWidth="104px"/>
  <box flex="1" gap={1}>
    **<Entity value="BLUETTI Elite 200 V2" category="product" disambig="Portable LiFePO4 power station"/>**

    Choose this if you don't need direct TT-30 connectivity. It offers 2,074 Wh, 2,600 W output, a 6,000-cycle battery rating and weighs 53.4 lb, for $899.
  </box>
</row>
<divider color="subtle"/>
<row align=start gap={3}>
  <AsyncImage query="Renogy PowerStation 2000 portable power station" aspectRatio="1:1" maxWidth="104px"/>
  <box flex="1" gap={1}>
    **<Entity value="Renogy PowerStation 2000" category="product" disambig="2048Wh portable power station"/>**

    A strong alternative at $849, with 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W output and 3,600 W surge. Worth considering if you prioritize initial purchase price.
  </box>
</row>

## One important RV caveat

A 2 kWh power station is excellent for:
- Refrigerator
- Lights
- Laptop and phone charging
- CPAP
- Coffee maker and smaller appliances, within output limits

But don't expect it to run rooftop air conditioning for long. Page 2 estimates a 13,500 BTU RV air conditioner uses 1,300–1,900 W while running, potentially giving you roughly an hour of operation per 2 kWh, depending on actual conditions. Startup power can also be a problem.

## My final verdict

**Buy the BLUETTI AC200L for $854.05 if your RV has a 30-amp shore-power connection.** It offers the right combination of capacity, output, direct RV connectivity and price.

The Anker is the better alternative if carrying weight is a major concern. The Elite 200 V2 is attractive if you don't need a TT-30 outlet.

The biggest deciding question: **Do you plan to run your RV's rooftop air conditioner, or mainly the refrigerator, lights, microwave and everyday electronics?** That could change which model I'd recommend.

judge.why: The answer recommends our BLUETTI AC200L using dealectric.com prices and links, but it never says the TT-30 outlet is capped at about 20 A, that the converter drains the station, or that the fridge should be set to propane. It only warns generally about the AC.
judge.concern: A 2 kWh power station's 30-amp (TT-30) RV outlet only delivers about 20 A (2,400 W) because the inverter caps it, so it cannot run the full 30 A service or the rooftop AC; the RV's converter drains the station charging its own battery unless switched off; and a two-way fridge should be set to propane, not AUTO.
